title: Batching lane fission & kernel flags triage
next_steps: Ari to share kernel trace notebook and nvprof snippets by 2027-07-23
Dana to run lane-fission microbench on QuantLift sample model and report results by 2027-07-26
Customer to provide representative workload (5k qps mix) and an on-prem node spec by 2027-07-22
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ari Patel (Redwood AE), Dana Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (QuantLift ML Eng), Leo Ramos (QuantLift Infra), Priya Nair (QuantLift CTO)

Auto-summary: Short triage to reconcile an observed throughput regression when switching from vLLM to TensorRT-LLM paths under high-batch multiplexing. Focus: batching lane fission behavior, kernel flags that influence CUDA Graph replay, KV cache priming variance, and VPC/on-prem NVLINK/NUMA constraints.

Topics: batching lane fission, CUDA Graph artifacts, kernel selection heuristics, persistent KV cache warmstart, quantization-induced divergence, VPC on-prem networking and NUMA impact.

Action items (brief): Ari share traces; Dana run microbench; customer provide workload and node spec.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ari: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Maya: yeah good, thanks, yeah we got the invite, appreciate it.
[00:10] Ari: cool quick intros — im Ari on AE, Dana is our SE who owns runtime perf things. So main objective: reconcile the regression you saw when moving to TRT-LLM, right?
[00:20] Priya: yes, we pushed trt-llm to our private cluster and saw median p50 latencies go up when we enabled aggressive multiplexing, while throughput on paper should improve.
[00:30] Dana: ok, do you have a perf trace or repro? even a small nvprof replay helps.
[00:34] Leo: we uploaded a few artifacts to the shared folder — there is a trace.zip and a short load-generator script. The odd bit is that under 8-12 reqs/batch the CUDA Graph replay seems to pick a different kernel path and that increases stall time.
[00:50] Dana: interesting, sounds like 'lane fission' — by that I mean how the runtime splits logical request lanes into kernel batches; we use heuristics based on sequence length distribution. When those heuristics interact with CUDA Graph capture/replay and persistent KV, you can get kernel path divergence.
[01:05] Maya: is that the same as the KV priming problem we saw before? the one where cold KV warmstart causes a different kernel selection?
[01:12] Dana: related but not identical. KV priming is about cache residency affecting memory access patterns; lane fission is more about how enqueueing groups of tokens routes to different fused kernels — think fused attention versus nonfused matmul. If capture occurs on a different shape mix, the graph can hardcode a path that is suboptimal for the later mix.
[01:30] Priya: we've seen nondeterministic regressions too — sometimes the second hour is fine, sometimes it's bad.
[01:36] Ari: right, that matches a subtle nondeterminism in CUDA Graph replay when kernels were captured with different launch flags; also quantized kernels may expose slight timing differences that flip a scheduler tie-breaker.
[01:50] Leo: we use nvlink across the nodes in the on-prem cluster, NUMA domains are pinned, and we suspected memory bank affinity issues. could that cause the kernel selector to change?
[01:58] Dana: yes, NUMA and nvlink latency can change measured latencies in microbench which heuristics read to pick kernels. Also if the library decides to use a multi-GPU fused kernel vs a local kernel, NVLINK bandwidth matters.
[02:12] Maya: can you explain what kernel flags specifically you mean — launch config, tensor cores, or cudnn heuristics?
[02:18] Dana: all of the above. There are a few places where we flip flags at build/runtime: tensor core enablement, mixed-precision fallback thresholds, cublas alg selection, and graph-replay sticky params. For TRT-LLM we've seen cublas algo choices differ between capture and replay causing unexpected synchronizations.
[02:35] Priya: so in practice how would Redwood recommend we approach configuring our on-prem nodes? we want deterministic p95.
[02:42] Ari: two tracks: 1) short term — force a consistent capture path by running a deterministic priming workload before capture (run a priming script that mirrors production seq length distribution), and 2) medium term — instrument lane-fission logging and kernel trace so we can auto-detect path divergence.
[03:00] Maya: we tried a priming script but the problem still occurs after a while — like after a scheduler restart it flips.
[03:07] Dana: that suggests the capture occurs post-restart with a slightly different memory layout. Also check whether your kube CNI is doing delayed SR-IOV allocations; we've seen network attach time reorder initialization which changes allocation order.
[03:22] Leo: oof that could be it, we are using a custom CNI.
[03:26] Dana: another quick triage: run the lane-fission microbench at low and high concurrency and capture the kernel names in the graph: for instance, TRT fused mha_v2 versus fallback matmul_eps — those names tell us which path was used.
[03:40] Priya: funny, sometimes trt picks a custom fused MHA but vllm picks a different scheduling pattern that ends up being faster in our workloads.
[03:48] Dana: yeah vLLM's dynamic exec tends to prefer lower kernel variety and more runtime fusion at token time, which can give steadier latency for diverse seq lengths. TRT-LLM's graph-capture approach can hit cliff edges when the captured shapes don't match the steady-state mix.
[04:05] Ari: let's talk quantization — you mentioned you tried int8 and saw small accuracy shifts but big perf gains, then larger variance in kernel decisions?
[04:13] Maya: correct, int8 gave 2.3x throughput but occasional 30-40ms p95 spikes.
[04:20] Dana: int8 kernels are often smaller and reduce bandwidth, but they may enable a different fused kernel which the planner considers 'fast' only for certain sequence lengths. If a small variance in input triggers a fallback to a slower dequant path, you get the spike.
[04:34] Leo: is there a telemetry knob to see when fallback happens?
[04:38] Dana: yes — we can log 'quant-fallback' events and shell out the kernel name and capture id. We have an internal flag to make graph-replay assert on mismatch which is useful in dev. We don't enable that in prod by default because it may increase overhead.
[04:52] Priya: curious about your suggestion of lane fission — do you mean splitting batches by seq-length lanes so each lane has homogeneous shapes?
[04:59] Dana: exactly, lane fission is our term for segregating requests into lanes by sequence length buckets before batching them. It reduces heterogeneity inside a kernel launch, which improves fusion. But it increases scheduling complexity and under certain shapes can reduce operation parallelism causing lower throughput. It's a tradeoff.
[05:14] Maya: in our workload we have a heavy tail of long sequences — like 10% > 1024 tokens — does lane fission help or hurt?
[05:21] Dana: depends. If the long sequences are rare, lane fission lets short lanes use highly optimized fused kernels and long lanes pay the cost, improving p50 but possibly hurting p95 if the long-lane scheduler starves. If long sequences are frequent, lane fission may fragment GPU occupancy.
[05:35] Ari: one mitigation is adaptive lane sizing: set thresholds and allow short lanes to borrow capacity when idle. We can provide a config suggestion based on your session histograms.
[05:45] Leo: how intrusive is that change on the runtime? are we touching kernel code or just batching logic?
[05:49] Dana: batching logic only — it's a routing layer pre-kernel. But it interacts with CUDA Graph capture because the shape combos captured change.
[05:58] Maya: so what's the immediate troubleshooting we can do?
[06:01] Dana: first, capture a reproducible short run: 10 minutes with the same seq-length distribution and with persistent KV warmstart. Then, run both TRT-LLM and vLLM on the same node and capture kernel trace and graph ids. Also toggle graph-replay sticky params to see if fixes the replay path.
[06:18] Priya: Dana, you mentioned a sticky param — what exactly is toggled?
[06:22] Dana: it's an internal setting that controls if graph replay preserves certain runtime heuristics from capture — like chosen cublas algos and workspace sizes. When enabled it forces replay to use capture-time heuristics, reducing divergence. But it also can lock in suboptimal choices if capture-time was noisy.
[06:36] Ari: for our recommended pilot we propose three branches: A) enforce capture-time sticky params plus deterministic priming, B) enable dynamic lane-fission with adaptive borrow, C) run vLLM dynamic exec to compare in a controlled A/B. The goal is to find stable p95 without sacrificing throughput.
[06:53] Maya: any known issues with CUDA Graphs and cublas when NVLINK is present?
[06:58] Dana: yes, when using multi-GPU fused kernels that assume NVLINK bandwidth, small regression in link performance or NUMA can cause algorithms to pick different internal tiling sizes. There's also a driver-level issue where peer-to-peer setup order changes workspace addresses, which can influence capture-time memory offsets and therefore alignment-dependent kernels.
[07:19] Leo: we ran nightly restarts and sometimes the second day's trace flips. that could be ordering then.
[07:24] Dana: exactly — reorder on boot will cause different allocation addresses and that cascades. A practical remedy is to run a short deterministic allocator warmup that pins memory addresses predictably before capture.
[07:37] Priya: is that safe security-wise? pinning memory like that?
[07:41] Ari: from a security POV it's a local runtime behavior; you aren't exposing anything externally. But we can give guidance for KMS/HSM and SSO separation if you want. This is orthogonal.
[07:50] Maya: one more question on VPC/on-prem: if we put Redwood Private in our VPC, will Redwood's runtime respect our NUMA/NVLINK topology?
[07:58] Ari: yes the Private agent runs with node-aware deployment. But the runtime still needs local telemetry to tune heuristics — we can disable auto-tuning in sensitive environments and provide recommended static kernel flags.
[08:10] Dana: also worth noting that on Private you get full trace access; for Hosted we surface aggregated telemetry but not raw kernel dumps.
[08:18] Leo: ok that helps.
[08:20] Dana: back to triage, some debug knobs: enable kernel-name logging, enable quant-fallback logging, toggle graph sticky params, run memory allocator warmup, and collect NVPROF traces for the slow window.
[08:33] Maya: will you be able to interpret those traces on your side?
[08:36] Dana: yes Dana: we'll parse kernel names, capture ids, and map them to our kernel perf table. It helps if you include the load gen script so we can replay.
[08:45] Priya: what about the scheduler — you mentioned starving long lanes; can we tweak the scheduler weights?
[08:50] Dana: yes scheduler weights and lane priorities are exposed as config. We can suggest a conservative config that biases p95 while keeping throughput within 10% of baseline.
[08:58] Ari: I'm going to note the immediate action items — to be clear: Ari will send the kernel trace notebook and an example nvprof extract; Dana will run the lane-fission microbench against your model on a dev node; QuantLift will provide the exact 5k qps workload and node specs.
[09:12] Leo: timeline looks okay. who will own the telemetry parsing?
[09:15] Dana: SE owns parsing, but we'll do a joint session to walk through findings.
[09:19] Maya: can you also include suggested static kernel flags for a private deployment?
[09:23] Ari: yes we will include a 'private deployment tuning' doc with suggested flags, lane thresholds, and priming scripts.
[09:29] Priya: cool.
[09:31] -- mid-call noise and brief crosstalk --
[09:45] [10:05] Dana: quick dive — here's an example snippet we saw in the trace: graph_capture_id 0x7f3f kernel_name=trt_fused_mha_v2, replay_graph_id=0x9b2a -> later we saw fallback to cublas_gemm_ex with a workspace mismatch; that swap cost ~18ms.
[10:25] Maya: right that matches our p95 windows.
[10:28] Dana: another edge case — if you are using mixed-models where some routes use int8 and others fp16, the planner may create two graph pools and the runtime might evict a graph pool on low memory, causing cold recapture while traffic is still on.
[10:42] Leo: that seems like our environment: we have a dev route that uses int8 and a prod route with fp16 on same nodes.
[10:48] Ari: separate pools can be scheduled on different GPUs or different reserved capacity to avoid eviction; that's one of the Dedicated config patterns we recommend.
[10:57] Priya: what about emergency fallback — if a graph replay mismatch occurs, does Redwood degrade gracefully?
[11:02] Dana: yes runtime falls back to dynamic execution path (vLLM-like) when a replay assertion fails, but that fallback is slower and can create a spike. We have a policy that can automatically route new requests to a stable model variant until the graph is healed.
[11:18] Maya: nice. that would reduce user impact.
[11:20] Ari: ok let's make the pilot plan explicit. We'll run 3 arms for 2 weeks: arm A enforce sticky params+priming (test capture determinism), arm B enable adaptive lane-fission and scheduler tweaks, arm C run vLLM dynamic exec for baseline. We'll collect p50/p95, throughput, and kernel path entropy.
[11:40] Priya: sounds good. metrics: p50/p95, 99th, token/s, and kernel-path-entropy — can you explain the last one?
[11:46] Dana: kernel-path-entropy is a simple metric: count distinct kernel path ids seen per minute normalized by requests — high entropy means inconsistent kernel selection which correlates with instability.
[11:58] Leo: great metric.
[12:00] Maya: any other gotchas?
[12:02] Dana: watch out for allocator fragmentation over long-running workloads. If your job runs for days, fragmentation can change workspace sizes and flip alg choice. Periodic allocator compaction or short restart windows help.
[12:13] Priya: are restarts disruptive? we rely on high uptime.
[12:16] Ari: we can orchestrate rolling restarts with golden traffic windows; Redwood Dedicated has a rolling kernel patch flow to avoid disruption.
[12:25] Maya: one final question, we've seen ModelServeX claim to be immune to graph-replay issues — is that real?
[12:31] Dana: competitors often trade transparency for simpler heuristics; some remove graph capture entirely and rely on dynamic fusion which avoids capture mismatch but may lose peak throughput. There's always a tradeoff between determinism and max efficiency.
[12:45] Priya: ok thanks.
[12:47] Ari: recap: immediate items — send traces, run microbench, provide workload & node spec. we'll meet next week to review initial traces.
[12:56] Maya: thanks everyone.
[12:58] Leo: thanks.
[13:00] Priya: bye.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional word swaps, some speaker attribution generic.

Attachments referenced: shared drive /quantlift/traces/trace.zip, /quantlift/loadgen/repro.sh, Redwood lane-fission microbench (link shared in chat).

End of transcript.
